summary: This standards-track memo defines a DHCPv4 option, modelled on the DHCPv6 Rapid Commit option, that lets a client and server finish configuration in two messages instead of the usual four. This speeds up how quickly a client gets its address and settings.

eli5.summary: Getting a network address normally takes four back-and-forth steps. This option lets a computer and server skip ahead and finish in two, like ordering with a single exchange.

questions: how many messages does dhcp rapid commit use
when should i enable rapid commit on a dhcp server
subtitle: A DHCPv4 option that lets a client get its address in two messages instead of four.

tldr.problem: The normal DHCPv4 exchange takes four messages. In places where clients move often and attach to new networks frequently, that delay is unwelcome, and the protection the longer exchange offers may not be needed.
tldr.mechanism: A client puts a Rapid Commit option (code 80) in its DHCPDISCOVER. A server that is configured to allow it answers directly with a DHCPACK carrying the same option and a fully committed address, skipping the offer and request steps.
tldr.outcome: Clients are configured faster, but the server commits an address for every such client. It should only be enabled when one server serves the subnet or when every server has plenty of addresses, and it makes address exhaustion easier to cause.

today: RFC 4039 is a Proposed Standard from March 2005. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Two Messages Can Be Enough
sections.content:
In environments with high mobility, where the network attachment point changes frequently, it helps to configure clients quickly. RFC 4039 observes that in such places the protections of the normal 4-message exchange may not be needed.

The 4-message exchange lets several DHCP servers cooperate without wasting addresses, because addresses are only provisionally assigned until the client chooses one and requests it. A 2-message exchange may therefore be used when only one server is present, or when addresses are plentiful and having several servers commit addresses for one client is not a problem.

The new Rapid Commit option is modeled on the DHCPv6 Rapid Commit option from RFC 3315. If the server does not agree to use it, it simply handles the DHCPDISCOVER as defined in RFC 2131.
sections.eli5: Usually you ask for an address, get offers, pick one and then get a final yes. If you are the only one asking and there are plenty of addresses, you can skip the middle steps.

sections.title: How Client and Server Use the Option
sections.content:
A client that wants rapid commit includes a Rapid Commit option in the DHCPDISCOVER messages it sends. It MUST NOT include the option in any other message. Both client and server only use the option when configured to do so.

The client still processes responses as in RFC 2131. But if it receives a DHCPACK with a Rapid Commit option, it SHOULD process that DHCPACK immediately, without waiting for further DHCPOFFER or DHCPACK messages, and use the address and configuration in it.

A server that supports the option MAY answer such a DHCPDISCOVER with a DHCPACK that includes the Rapid Commit option and fully committed address and configuration information. A server MUST NOT include the option in any other message. The option MUST NOT appear in a Parameter Request List option (RFC 2132).

The server decides. It may ignore the option and send an ordinary DHCPOFFER, and the client then continues with the usual four-message exchange.
sections.eli5: The client says 'I would take an address right away, if you are willing'. A willing server hands one over and writes it down. An unwilling server just makes an offer the usual way.

sections.title: The Revised Step-by-Step Flow
sections.content:
The RFC rewrites the six-step flow of Section 3.1 of RFC 2131 to include rapid commit. The client broadcasts a DHCPDISCOVER, with the Rapid Commit option if it wants it. Each server answers with either a DHCPOFFER or, only if the DISCOVER carried the option and local policy allows it, a DHCPACK with the Rapid Commit option.

A server sending the DHCPACK commits the binding to persistent storage before sending it. When allocating a new address, servers SHOULD check that it is not already in use, for example by probing it with an ICMP Echo Request, and administrators MAY disable these probes.

If the client gets a DHCPACK with Rapid Commit and the parameters are acceptable, it may go straight to the final step. Otherwise it picks a server and broadcasts a DHCPREQUEST as before. In the final step the client SHOULD perform a last check such as ARP. If the address is already in use, it MUST send a DHCPDECLINE and restart configuration, and it SHOULD wait at least ten seconds before restarting. A DHCPNAK also makes the client restart.

The client may later give up its lease with a DHCPRELEASE, using the same 'client identifier' it used to obtain the lease.
sections.eli5: The client shouts for an address. If a server answers 'yours is 10, written down', the client does a quick check that nobody else is using it and starts using it. If the check fails, it says no thanks and tries again after a short wait.

sections.title: Administrative Considerations
sections.content:
Because a Rapid Commit server commits a binding for every client that asks, administrators MUST only enable the option on a server when one of two conditions holds. Either the server is the only server for the subnet, or, when several servers are present, each may commit a binding for all clients and therefore each must have enough addresses available.

A server MAY also allow a different, likely shorter, initial lease time for addresses assigned using Rapid Commit. This helps to reclaim addresses that clients never actually use.
sections.eli5: Handing out an address to everyone who asks only works if you have enough to go round. A shorter first loan lets the server get unused ones back sooner.

sections.title: The Rapid Commit Option Format
sections.content:
The option is very small. Its code is 80 and its length is 0, so it has no data and its presence is the signal.

A client MUST include it in a DHCPDISCOVER if it is prepared to perform the DHCPDISCOVER-DHCPACK exchange. A server MUST include it in the DHCPACK it sends in response to such a DHCPDISCOVER when completing that exchange. IANA has assigned value 80 in accordance with RFC 2939.
sections.eli5: It is a tiny flag with a number on it and nothing inside. Seeing the flag is enough to know what is wanted.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the concepts do not significantly alter the security considerations of DHCP (see RFC 2131 and RFC 3118). There is one exception: the option could help denial of service attacks.

A mischievous client could use up all available addresses more rapidly. It could also do so without needing two-way communication, because injecting DHCPDISCOVER messages carrying the Rapid Commit option is enough to make a server allocate an address.
sections.eli5: If a server gives away an address to anyone who asks, a troublemaker can ask over and over and use them all up faster.
